label: pp-funding-bioelectricity-organism-design
topic: Funding and institutions in bioelectricity and organism design, including the Levin ecosystem; and the idea of an optogenetic xenobot
summary: Money behind xenobots/anthrobots traces to four verifiable streams: the Paul G. Allen Frontiers Group / Allen Family Foundation (Allen Discovery Center at Tufts, announced March 2016), DARPA (award HR0011-18-2-0022, the Lifelong-Learning-Machines-era contract number as printed in Crossref funder metadata), NSF, and for the 2023 anthrobot paper the John Templeton Foundation (award 62212) and NIH (S10 OD021624). The Wyss Institute (Harvard) is a Levin affiliation funded mainly by gifts from Hansjorg Wyss (USD 125M 2009, 125M 2013, 131M 2019, 350M 2022 per Harvard Magazine / Crimson). The Institute for Computationally Designed Organisms (icdorgs.org) is a two-site collaboration (Tufts Allen Center + UVM) whose own site does not state its funding. I could not find a dedicated 'bioelectricity foundation' with fetched evidence. Optogenetics in this field: published peer-reviewed optogenetic work on epidermal multiciliated cells (Yasunaga 2022, phytochrome PHYB/PIF) controls rootlet anchoring, not beating; the only light-gated beating claim I saw (ChR2 in ciliated biobots) came from a search-engine snippet of a US patent (12215344) that I could not open (USPTO PDF came back corrupt), so it is unverified. The closest peer-reviewed light-driven contractile biohybrid is Park 2016 (Science, optogenetic cardiomyocyte stingray). A computation-only first step is a design/simulation study (not run here).
lay_summary: Most of the money behind the 'living robots' made from frog cells came from a private foundation set up by Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen, from the US military research agency DARPA, and from the US National Science Foundation. The later robots made from human lung cells were also backed by the John Templeton Foundation and the NIH. Harvard's Wyss Institute, which is paid for mostly by gifts from one Swiss billionaire, is a partner. The idea of steering these robots with light means giving their hair-like cilia a light switch, like adding a remote control to a tiny rowing crew. I found one patent claim that this works, but I could not open it, so I treat it as unconfirmed. A sensible first step would be to simulate the design on a computer before touching any cells.

findings.claim: Peer-reviewed optogenetics on Xenopus multiciliated cells (Yasunaga 2022, Nat Commun) used the phycocyanobilin PHYB/PIF system (660 nm red associates, 740 nm far-red dissociates) to disrupt Ezrin and rootlet tilting; it reported no light-controlled ciliary beating.
findings.evidence_quote: Far-red exposure disrupted rootlet tilting, revealed by shortening of the apparent rootlet length.

findings.claim: That study was funded by DFG (WA 597/20-1, SFB 1453, Emmy-Noether) and Else Kroner-Fresenius-Stiftung, i.e. outside the Levin ecosystem.

findings.claim: Park et al. 2016 (Science, phototactic soft-robotic ray; optogenetically controlled engineered cardiomyocytes) is the established precedent for light-driven contractile tissue; Crossref funders include Wyss Institute, NSF, ONR, NCATS, MacArthur Foundation, Army Research Lab.
findings.evidence_quote: title: Phototactic guidance of a tissue-engineered soft-robotic ray (that it uses optogenetic cardiomyocytes is background knowledge; abstract not fetched)

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED: a US patent (12215344, 'Engineered multicellular ciliated organisms and kinematic self-replication thereof') is reported by a search summary to describe ChR2 mRNA-injected biobots with blue light raising velocity (n=8 per group, p=0.0124). I could not open it: the USPTO PDF downloads were corrupt (two different sizes) and Google Patents returned 503.
A Europe PMC search for (optogenetic OR channelrhodopsin) AND (cilia) AND (beating OR motility) returned 294 hits; in the first 15 shown none was a Xenopus biobot light-gated cilia-beating study.

recommendations: Computation-only first step: (1) in silico design of an optogenetic xenobot: a voxel/cilia-patch model (as in the Kriegman 2020 design pipeline) where each ciliated patch has a light-gated on/off state and a light field is the only input; (2) use evolutionary search to find patch layouts and light patterns that give steerable swimming and test robustness to noise in channel expression and light attenuation; (3) pre-register predicted velocities before any wet work; (4) use published ChR2 kinetics and Yasunaga/cilia-beat data as parameters (requires fetching, not done here).

What would be new: closed-loop-free light steering of ciliated Xenopus-derived biobots (no imaging, no manipulation) with peer-reviewed data; the patent claim, if real, may already cover open-loop ChR2 velocity increase, so freedom-to-operate and prior art must be checked after obtaining the full text.
Obtain patent 12215344 text via a working source and verify the ChR2 claim before relying on it.
